**ATP**. In complex V (the oxysome) of the inner mitochondrial membrane, the \(\text{F}_0\) part channels protons into the inner chamber, and this is coupled to the catalytic site of \(\text{F}_1\), which synthesises ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate (oxidative phosphorylation).

**In man**, anaerobic respiration occurs in the **skeletal muscles** during very fast and severe work (vigorous exercise), when sufficient oxygen is not immediately available to the muscle fibres. Glucose is broken down by glycolysis to pyruvic acid, which is reduced to **lactic acid**; the lactic acid accumulates and causes muscle fatigue, and during rest it is reconverted to pyruvic acid and sent back into aerobic respiration. Erythrocytes also depend on glycolysis alone for their energy.

**In yeast**, anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is absent, for example in a glucose solution sealed from air. Pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, which is reduced to **ethanol**, and \(\text{CO}_2\) is released (alcoholic fermentation). When oxygen is present, yeast respires aerobically.

In both, the first stage, glycolysis, takes place in the **cytoplasm** of the cell.
[Note: the chapter places glycolysis in the cytoplasm but does not state where pyruvic acid is converted to lactic acid or ethanol.]
[Note: the textbook also lists the brain among tissues for which glycolysis is the only source of energy; the brain normally obtains its energy by aerobic oxidation of glucose.]

In anaerobic respiration glucose is only **incompletely oxidised**. Glycolysis gives a net gain of only 2 ATP (4 ATP formed by substrate-level phosphorylation minus 2 ATP used), and the \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) it forms is used to reduce pyruvic acid to lactic acid (or acetaldehyde to ethanol) instead of being oxidised in the electron transport chain. Much of the energy of glucose therefore remains locked in lactic acid or ethanol. In aerobic respiration glucose is completely oxidised through the link reaction, Krebs cycle and ETS, and the ETS alone forms 34 of the net 38 ATP.

The **inner mitochondrial membrane**. The electron carriers and enzymes of the ETS are arranged on it in the form of complexes I, II, III, IV and V, and oxidative phosphorylation occurs on this membrane only.
**Molecular oxygen** (\(\text{O}_2\)). Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) transfers the electrons to molecular oxygen in terminal oxidation, and the reduced oxygen combines with protons to form water.

**Respiratory quotient (RQ)**, or respiratory ratio, is the ratio of the volume of \(\text{CO}_2\) released to the volume of \(\text{O}_2\) consumed in respiration:
\(\text{RQ} = \dfrac{\text{volume of CO}_2\text{ released}}{\text{volume of O}_2\text{ consumed}}\)
Its value depends on the type of respiratory substrate. For **fats** the RQ is less than 1, mostly about **0.7**, because the volume of \(\text{CO}_2\) released is less than the volume of \(\text{O}_2\) consumed.

**Respiratory substrates** are the complex organic substances that are oxidised in cellular respiration to simple components to release biological energy. Carbohydrates, fats and proteins can all be used: besides glucose, amino acids from protein metabolism and fatty acids from lipid metabolism enter the Krebs cycle through acetyl CoA. The most common respiratory substrate is the carbohydrate **glucose**.
[Note: the chapter does not say in so many words that glucose is the most common respiratory substrate; it describes respiration throughout as the oxidation of glucose.]

**i. Glycolysis**
- Glycolysis is the breakdown of one glucose molecule into two molecules of pyruvic acid. It is the common first step of both anaerobic and aerobic respiration and occurs in the **cytoplasm**.
- It is completed in **ten steps** grouped into two phases.
- **Preparatory phase** (first five steps): glucose is phosphorylated twice at the cost of 2 ATP to form fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, which splits into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (two isomeric trioses). Dihydroxyacetone phosphate is isomerised, so two molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate are formed.
- **Pay-off phase**: each glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is oxidised and phosphorylated with inorganic phosphate (not ATP) to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, forming \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\). Through a series of reactions these are converted to two pyruvic acid molecules, and the energy released forms 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
- Net gain per glucose: **2 ATP** and **2 \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\)**.
- Glycolysis is under tight control by enzymes such as hexokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase, and by the hormones glucagon, epinephrine and insulin.

**ii. Fermentation by yeast**
- In the absence of oxygen yeast respires anaerobically; this is **alcoholic fermentation**.
- Glucose is first broken down by glycolysis into two molecules of pyruvic acid, forming \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\).
- Pyruvate is decarboxylated to **acetaldehyde**, releasing \(\text{CO}_2\).
- Acetaldehyde is reduced by \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) to **ethanol**, which regenerates \(\text{NAD}^+\).
- \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \rightarrow 2\,\text{CH}_3\text{COCOOH} \rightarrow 2\,\text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + 2\,\text{CO}_2 \rightarrow 2\,\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\) (glucose, pyruvic acid, acetaldehyde, ethanol).
- Accumulation of ethanol in a yeast culture may stop further multiplication and lead to the death of the cells. In the presence of oxygen yeast respires aerobically.
- Fermentation is used in bakeries and distilleries and in the commercial production of alcohol.

**iii. Electron transport chain**
- The electron carriers and enzymes are arranged on the **inner mitochondrial membrane** as complexes I, II, III, IV and V.
- \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) is oxidised by complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) by complex II (succinate dehydrogenase); their electrons pass to ubiquinone (coenzyme Q), which becomes ubiquinol. The protons are released into the outer chamber.
- Complex III (cytochrome \(\text{bc}_1\) complex) passes electrons to cytochrome c, a mobile carrier, which carries them to complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase).
- Complex IV transfers the electrons to **molecular oxygen** (terminal oxidation), and reduced oxygen combines with protons to form **water**.
- Protons flow back into the inner chamber through the \(\text{F}_0\) part of complex V, and \(\text{F}_1\) synthesises ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate: **oxidative phosphorylation**, called chemiosmosis by Peter Mitchell.
- Each \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) yields 3 ATP and each \(\text{FADH}_2\) 2 ATP; 34 of the 38 ATP from one glucose come from the ETS.
[Note: the textbook's equation for alcoholic fermentation shows a single \(\text{CO}_2\); two molecules of pyruvic acid release two.]

The three stages form one continuous pathway of aerobic respiration, linked by their products.
1. **Glycolysis** in the cytoplasm breaks one glucose molecule into two molecules of **pyruvic acid**, forming 2 ATP (net) and 2 \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\).
2. Pyruvic acid enters the mitochondrion, where the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts it to **acetyl CoA** with release of \(\text{CO}_2\) and formation of \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\). This is the 'connecting link' reaction between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.
3. In the **TCA (Krebs) cycle** in the mitochondrial matrix, acetyl CoA condenses with oxaloacetic acid to form citric acid, which is oxidised step by step, releasing \(\text{CO}_2\) and regenerating oxaloacetic acid. Its four dehydrogenation steps reduce coenzymes to \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\), and one GTP (ATP) is formed per turn.
4. The \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) produced in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle are oxidised in the **electron transport chain** on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their electrons pass through complexes I to IV to molecular oxygen, forming water, and oxidative phosphorylation forms ATP.
5. The ETS in turn regenerates the oxidised coenzymes (\(\text{NAD}^+\) and FAD) so that glycolysis and the Krebs cycle can continue.
Thus glycolysis supplies pyruvic acid to the TCA cycle, both supply reduced coenzymes to the ETS, and the ETS produces 34 of the 38 ATP from one glucose molecule.
[Note: the textbook writes the oxidised form of FAD as \(\text{FAD}^+\); it is FAD.]

**Anaerobic respiration of yeast** can be shown by the chapter's experiment.
1. Add a pinch of dry baker's yeast suspended in water (or a few ml of bakery yeast suspension) to about 10 ml of 10 percent glucose solution in a test tube (tube A).
2. Cover the surface of the liquid carefully with oil to prevent contact with air, and close the tube tightly with a rubber stopper.
3. Through the stopper insert a short bent glass tube reaching the air in the tube, and connect it by rubber tubing to a delivery tube whose open end dips into lime water in a second test tube (tube B). Fit both stoppers tightly.
4. Keep tube A in warm water (\(37^{\circ}\text{C}\) to \(38^{\circ}\text{C}\)) in a beaker.
5. The lime water gradually turns **milky**, showing that \(\text{CO}_2\) is evolved. The level of lime water in the delivery tube does **not rise**, so there is no fall in the volume of gas in tube A and no oxygen is used.
6. After a day or two, opening tube A gives a **smell of alcohol**, showing that ethanol has formed. Yeast has therefore respired anaerobically, fermenting glucose to ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\).

**Aerobic respiration**: the chapter states that in the presence of oxygen yeast respires aerobically. The comparison needs a second tube set up in the same way but without the oil layer, so that the yeast suspension is in contact with air.
[Note: the chapter describes only the anaerobic set-up and gives no procedure or observations for showing aerobic respiration in yeast, although it introduces its experiments under the heading that aerobic respiration can be demonstrated by them.]

Releasing energy step by step serves several purposes.
1. A stepwise release of chemical bond energy allows a relatively **higher proportion of that energy to be used in ATP synthesis**.
2. The enzymes of different steps can be enhanced or inhibited by specific compounds, so the **rate of the pathway and the energy output can be controlled** according to the need of the cell.
3. The same pathway can supply **intermediates used to synthesise other biomolecules**, such as amino acids.
4. In the ETS, stepwise release of energy **prevents damage to the cells**.

The **electron transport system (ETS)** oxidises the \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) formed during glycolysis, the connecting link reaction and the Krebs cycle, with the help of electron carriers and enzymes arranged on the **inner mitochondrial membrane** as complexes I, II, III, IV and V.
1. **Complex I** (NADH dehydrogenase) oxidises \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) and passes its electrons to **ubiquinone** (coenzyme Q, CoQ) on the inner membrane; reduced ubiquinone is called ubiquinol.
2. **Complex II** (succinate dehydrogenase) oxidises \(\text{FADH}_2\), and these electrons also go to CoQ.
3. During these oxidations electrons and protons are released, but only the electrons are carried forward; the protons are released into the **outer chamber** of the mitochondrion.
4. **Complex III** (cytochrome \(\text{bc}_1\) complex) oxidises ubiquinol and passes the electrons to **cytochrome c**, a small iron-containing protein loosely associated with the inner membrane, which acts as a mobile carrier between complexes III and IV.
5. **Complex IV** (cytochrome c oxidase, made of cytochromes a and \(\text{a}_3\)) oxidises cytochrome c and transfers the electrons to **molecular oxygen**. This is **terminal oxidation**; the reduced oxygen reacts with protons to form **water**.
6. The protons are channelled from the outer chamber back into the inner chamber by the \(\text{F}_0\) part of the oxysome (**complex V**). This is coupled to the catalytic site of \(\text{F}_1\), which synthesises ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate: **oxidative phosphorylation**. Because proton transfer is accompanied by ATP synthesis, Peter Mitchell named the process **chemiosmosis**.
7. Oxidation of one \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) gives 3 ATP and of one \(\text{FADH}_2\) gives 2 ATP, though the number depends on physiological conditions and the respiratory substrate.

**Significance**: the ETS produces 34 of the 38 ATP from one glucose molecule, regenerates the oxidised coenzymes for recycling, produces water and releases energy stepwise so that the cells are not damaged.

A pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism is called **amphibolic**. Respiration is usually described as a catabolic (oxidative) pathway, but this is not entirely correct, especially for the Krebs cycle.
- **Catabolic role**: the reactions of the Krebs cycle oxidise the acetyl part of acetyl CoA step by step, releasing energy and \(\text{CO}_2\). The same cycle is a common oxidative pathway for carbohydrates, fats and proteins, since glucose, fatty acids and amino acids all enter it through acetyl CoA.
- **Anabolic role**: as needed, acetyl CoA and some intermediates are drawn off as precursors for synthesis. Acetyl CoA is used to make **fatty acids**, \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate to make **glutamic acid** and oxaloacetate to make **aspartic acid**.
- Intermediates of the Krebs cycle therefore act as building blocks for other complex compounds, and the stepwise nature of the pathway allows the same route to supply intermediates for the synthesis of biomolecules such as amino acids.
Because the respiratory pathway both breaks down substrates to release energy and supplies raw materials for building new molecules, it is correctly called an amphibolic pathway rather than a purely catabolic one.

The Krebs cycle is called **amphibolic** because it takes part in both catabolism and anabolism. Its reactions oxidise the acetyl part of acetyl CoA step by step, releasing energy and \(\text{CO}_2\) (catabolism). At the same time, as per need, acetyl CoA, \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate are drawn off as precursors for the synthesis of fatty acids, glutamic acid and aspartic acid respectively (anabolism).

**Description**
Pyruvic acid entering the mitochondrion is oxidatively decarboxylated by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex to acetyl-CoA (2C), releasing \(\text{CO}_2\) and forming \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\). In the mitochondrial matrix, acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C), freeing CoA-SH. Aconitase converts citrate to isocitrate through cis-aconitate by removing and then adding water. Isocitrate dehydrogenase oxidises isocitrate to oxalosuccinic acid, which loses \(\text{CO}_2\) to give \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate (5C). The \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex then removes a second \(\text{CO}_2\) and adds CoA, forming succinyl-CoA (4C). Succinyl-CoA synthetase converts succinyl-CoA to succinate and forms one GTP (ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation. Succinate dehydrogenase oxidises succinate to fumarate, reducing FAD to \(\text{FADH}_2\); fumarase adds water to form malate, and malate dehydrogenase oxidises malate back to oxaloacetate, which completes the cycle. The four dehydrogenation steps produce three \(\text{NADH}+\text{H}^+\) and one \(\text{FADH}_2\) per turn, which pass their electrons to the electron transport chain. The cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule, and its intermediates are also used to build fatty acids and amino acids, so it is an amphibolic pathway.
